title: Krishna Emerges and the Villagers Rejoice
story:
The people of Vrindavan had been waiting on the bank of the Yamuna so long, and so still, that when Krishna finally rose out of the pool it was like the whole village drawing breath at once. Word had run through the lanes while he was gone, and the whole settlement had come down to the water to wait and watch and be afraid together. Their boy had leapt into the deep pool where the serpent Kaliya lived, into water made deadly by the serpent's poison. Now the serpent was gone and the water had settled, but no one on the bank had seen him go, and no one dared believe the boy would come back up. They had spent the long hours staring at the churning deep, and those who had gone down to the water's edge could find no sign of him in all that blackness. Nanda and Yashoda, who had raised him, had nearly lost their senses with dread.

He came up out of the water wearing a divine garland, his skin fragrant with sandal paste, his garment fine and bright. The cowherds, who had watched him vanish into the poison-dark pool and feared they would never see him again, rose to their feet as though their own breath had been given back to them. One after another they ran to him and embraced him — Yashoda and Nanda, Rohini the mother of Balarama, the gopis and the cowherd men — all of them holding him as though he had come back from the dead.

Balarama, his elder brother, laughed as he wrapped his arms around him. He alone had never doubted, for he knew what Krishna truly was, and there was a knowing joy in him, as if he had been waiting not for a rescue but for the game to end. The gopis, too, forgot their fear and broke into smiles, for the boy they had feared lost stood before them again, dripping and bright, as if nothing at all had happened.

And then the brahmanas came. The learned men of the settlement gathered around Nanda with their wives and their families, and they told him plainly what the moment required: “Give gifts to the twice-born, for the sake of the boy's deliverance.” For thanksgiving, in that world, was made with open hands, and Nanda gave as the occasion demanded — cows and gold, poured out for the life of his son — and the gifts went out to the learned ones as a father's gratitude made visible.

And Yashoda, the fortunate one who had lost her child and found him again, held Krishna close and would not let him go. The river ran sweet behind them, the poison gone with the serpent, and the village was whole again. They did not hurry home, but stood a while on the bank, letting the sweetness of the river and the nearness of the boy sink in.
reflection: The relief is physical before it is anything else — the whole village rising as though given back its breath. And the first response is not talk but giving: Nanda's cows and gold, poured out for his son's deliverance, as if gratitude needed to be made visible to be real.
next_story_tease: And soon the village would turn to its great autumn offering to Indra.
hero_scene: Krishna rising out of the Yamuna in a divine garland and bright garment, the cowherds and Yasoda and Nanda rushing to embrace him on the bank, Balarama laughing beside them.
visual_elements: the gopis and cowherds embracing him
cows and gold given in gratitude
